config.title: Intersection of Two Arrays

intro.title: Intersection of Two Arrays
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that finds the common elements between two arrays, known as the intersection. You will learn to implement this using a hash map (or object in JavaScript) to efficiently track and compare elements. The main technologies involved are JavaScript arrays, objects, and loops. This exercise will help you practice lesson-solving with data structures while writing clean, functional code.
intro.usecase: Finding common elements between datasets is essential for features like e-commerce product filtering, where you need to show items matching multiple customer preferences. Social media platforms use array intersections to display mutual friends between users or common interests in connection suggestions. In analytics dashboards, this pattern helps identify overlapping user segments across different marketing campaigns. Database query optimization and caching systems frequently intersect result sets to efficiently retrieve relevant records.

objectives: Implement a function that finds common elements between two arrays
Apply filtering logic to identify intersecting values
Construct a solution that handles arrays of varying lengths
Manipulate array data structures to extract matching elements
Initialize and populate a new array with intersection results
Configure comparison operations between array elements
Integrate array methods to create an intersection algorithm

content.body: Welcome! In this lesson, we'll find common elements between two arrays. You'll learn how to efficiently discover what numbers appear in both lists using a clever memory technique. Let's get started!
content.title: Introduction

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
1. Explain why checking every element against every other element is inefficient
2. Implement a lookup structure to remember seen values
3. Write a function that finds the intersection of two arrays in a single pass
4. Determine what to store as keys versus values in your lookup structure
5. Decide when to check the structure versus add to it
content.title: What you'll learn
Try it
content.prompt: Which numbers appear in BOTH arrays?
content.successMessage: Great! You found that 2 and 3 appear in both arrays.

content.title: Try a bigger array
content.prompt: Find the common numbers between these arrays
content.successMessage: Well done! You identified 4, 9, and 12 as the common elements.

content.title: One more
content.prompt: What numbers are in both lists?
content.successMessage: Excellent! You checked each element and found that 5 and 10 appear in both arrays.

content.body: What you just did was a brute force approach: for each element in the first array, you checked if it exists in the second array by scanning through it. This works for small arrays but becomes inefficient as they grow larger.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When both arrays have thousands of elements, checking every element against every other element becomes extremely slow. We need a smarter method that avoids repeated scanning. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: The core idea is to remember what we have already seen. Instead of scanning the second array repeatedly, we can use a lookup structure (like an object or Map) to store elements we've encountered. This way, checking if an element exists becomes a single, fast operation.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Think of it like a notebook where we write down what we've seen. When we encounter a new number, we first check our notebook to see if we've already written it down. If we have, we know it's a common element!

content.body: We'll use a single pass through the first array to build our 'memory notebook' (a lookup structure), then a single pass through the second array to check against it. This avoids the nested scanning of the brute force approach.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
Let's find intersection of [1, 2, 3, 4] and [3, 4, 5, 6]:
1. Create empty notebook (object)
2. Pass through first array: add 1, 2, 3, 4 to notebook
3. Pass through second array: check 3 → in notebook! Add to result. Check 4 → in notebook! Add to result. Check 5 → not in notebook. Check 6 → not in notebook.
4. Result: [3, 4]

content.body:
1. Create an empty lookup structure (object) to remember numbers
2. Go through the first array: for each number, add it to the lookup structure
3. Create an empty result array for common elements
4. Go through the second array: for each number, check if it exists in the lookup structure
5. If it exists, add it to the result array
6. Return the result array

content.body:
Congratulations! You've successfully implemented an efficient algorithm to find the intersection of two arrays. Key takeaways:
1. We use a lookup structure (object) as our 'memory notebook' to remember what we've seen
2. We store array elements as keys in the object (values are just markers like 'true')
3. We check the structure when processing the second array, not when building it
4. This approach avoids nested loops and works efficiently even for large arrays

Remember: The hashmap approach transforms an O(n²) brute force solution into an O(n) efficient one!
